chunks.text: To take us through sort of a high level of your response, and then I'm sure there'll be questions from the committee. Do you also just want to take a minute to introduce yourselves? Yes. We do have a board member who wished to dial in via Zoom. That's Erik Westergaard, our acting chair.

Great. We will make sure that we get him in as soon as we can, if he's there. He is here. Oh. Oh, excellent. Accept the promotion to the panel, Erik, and then we'll see your face. But do you want to kick us off while that happens in the background? Sure. I think Erik was going to give you a bit of an opening statement, but I can introduce myself-... and my colleagues if that's helpful.

Do that. So I'm Tim Sparks. I'm the general manager of Networks and System Change at the Authority. We have Grant Benvenuti, who is the manager of Network Policy at the Authority, and we have Nikolai Mumford, who is one of our senior legal counsel. Erik, can you hear me now?
Great.
I'll give him a minute.

Okay. Can everybody hear me? We can hear you. My apologies. Hello, I'm Erik Westergaard. Unlike Tim, I'm the deputy chair. We have recently had a new chair appointed to the Authority. I'd like to make an apology for our new chair not being able to attend.

He started today, and he's currently undertaking his Electricity Authority induction. You have our written evidence and our update. I'll take those documents as read. As a starter, I thought I'd be useful to provide some opening remarks about the Authority's Electricity Industry Participation Code and the Authority.

The Electricity Industry Act sets out the framework for the industry, for industry governance, and it includes establishing the Authority as an independent rule-making body, the scope of its rule-making powers, and the processes the Authority must follow when making or amending the Electricity Industry Participation Code, the rules of the electricity industry.

Since it was established in 2010, the Authority has focused on maintaining existing and making new rules necessary to operate the largest and most complex machine in New Zealand. We're doing this at a time of unprecedented change in the energy sector, and it's through these rules that we meet our main objective to promote competition, reliability, and the efficient operation of the electricity industry for the long-term benefit of consumers.

More recently, the Authority was given the additional objective of protecting the interests of domestic and small business consumers in relation to the supply of electricity. Mr Miller has made five complaints about different provisions of the code under various standing orders. In summary, Mr Miller thinks the code could be better in several areas. We agree. His complaint is that the code's inadequacy rises to the level of a breach of standing orders. We disagree for the reasons we set out in our written submissions.

The code needs to be kept under review and updated in response to new and changing technologies and business models. The Authority is consistently vigilant for opportunities to amend the code so it better promotes achievement of our main objective and the interests of consumers. When the Authority identifies a part of the code that no longer best promotes those outcomes, we act to amend it in a transparent and timely manner.

To amend the code, the Authority is generally required to consult and to assess the costs and benefits of proposed amendments. Many of the matters Mr Miller complains about are already being considered through the statutory process updating the code. Consultations are public, and we would welcome the submissions from Mr Miller on any of our code amendment proposals.

And we don't make these code changes alone. To aid the Authority in amending the code, the act requires the Authority to establish the Security and Reliability Council and at least one advisory group. Currently, the Authority has six industry working groups in operation.

In the last two and a half years, the Authority has made 52 code changes. And I note that this is more changes than in the previous five years. The pace of these changes reflects the changing nature of the industry. The Authority prioritizes its work based on the benefits of any amendment relative to others.

This prioritization applies to the issues raised by Mr Miller, and we have set out in our written submission some of the work the Authority is currently doing in this area. While we might have thoughts on the policy positions Mr Miller advocates for, until we have done work to develop a policy, including any related code amendments and consulted on it, we cannot be certain that the policy is the right one. We consider the regulatory framework and the act enables the Authority to address the policy issues raised by Mr Miller's complaint. That's all I have to say

in opening, and we're open to questions from the committee. For convenience, I will ask my fellow Authority team members to lead those questions. I will contribute as necessary. Thank you. Thank you, Erik. Thank you. Oh, there are a few questions. Some of them are specific, but I just want to clarify at the beginning.

So is the EA's contention that there is no public law jurisdiction for the Regulations Review Committee to consider your regulations? I wouldn't go so far to say there's no public law jurisdiction, but possibly. Some of the things that he's making complaints about are clearly things that have been made directly by Parliament.

Schedule 6, part 6A of the code, for example, was inserted directly into our code by Parliament. So I guess that raises a question about what would the jurisdiction of the Regulations Review Committee be to scrutinize that. We're not ruling out that you couldn't scrutinize it. I think it's just difficult to make that argument, that that scrutiny would lend itself to protecting Parliament's interest in ensuring those regulations represent what its intention was.

Does that make sense? Yep. So you say Eric's submission is consistent with the Regulations Review Committee being able to consider a complaint about your roles. Rather than making a jurisdictional argument by saying the committee can't look at these things, I think we'd rather say, if you are looking at them, take into account that Parliament very intentionally placed some of these provisions into the code and relatively recently.

So not much time has gone by and the circumstances haven't changed so much. Yeah. And the authority has taken steps to update those provisions where it has seen it necessary in the short term. Let's ask about some of those changes then. So, one of the first was the barriers to entry to small scale generation, and the response from EA was helpful on this point.

I just want to understand, it's somewhere where you've pointed to as a matter of policy that EA is continuing to work on. How will we know? What are the points in the review timeline for that for EA? If other consumers have this same experience, how does Parliament account to them that those changes are happening, and at what points?

Thanks, Chair. Yeah, that's a very good question. All our work program's public. We've just published this today, I think our updated statement of performance expectations for the coming year that has our current work program in it. As far as the work for small scale distributed generation goes, that's contained within a program of work we call our networks connections program. That's been running for about two years now.

There's already been a significant number of changes, and the last one was in May, which was the export changes to the export limits that raised those export limits. We're currently working on the next piece of that puzzle, which is around some minor clarifications to our policy intent and looking at balcony solar, which is obviously a topic of interest. And we don't talk publicly much about that, about any of those changes, before we get ready to release the paper. And the reason for that is staff are still developing

what our proposals are going to be. And until our board, who is the authority, until the board make the decision to consult, the board can change those at any time. So we do socialize what we're working on, but not the content of that until we're ready to release consultation papers. So the next one's in about September.

We're intending to go to the late August board meeting with that one, and that's the balcony solar one. And then there's another one which will intending to be just before the end of the calendar year, which looks at the detailed process itself for mainly residential consumers with rooftop solar, how the process they go through to apply and get that connected.

So that is the next big piece, once we get this little stuff through the mill. Just to add to that, I think it's important to remember that the authority is the expert body that Parliament has put in place to essentially determine what priorities should be given to what changes need to be made to electricity industry or the participation code.

We have, as we mentioned, consultations are generally public. Our work program is public. We are always open to submissions, including from Mr Miller, about what we should be focusing on, and we take any of those kinds of submissions seriously. But ultimately, we are accountable to Parliament.

We've been appointed. Yes. Yeah. Miles Emerson. Thanks, Chair. The new rule allowing distributors to allow exports of at least 10 kilowatts at individual connection points, unless this would compromise network reliability or safety. How are you tracking that? How do you track the percentage of rejections, just so you're getting an idea of whether the networks are being overly cautious or maybe putting some barriers in place to stop those

connections being connected to the grid? Thanks. Thanks, Chair. That change came into force, I think, on the 12th- 11th of May... 11th of May, yeah. Yeah. So it's only just come in. Just prior to Christmas, so nine months ago, we required all distributors to give us a whole lot of data on their connection processes, including things like processing time frames, declines, and that sort of thing.

And the intention is for us to use that. We're still going through the analysis of that data. It's a massive piece of data. Yeah. We're going to use that as a baseline. We are intending to go back out and refresh that data just around Christmas time to get the next 12 months' worth, and then we'll put a permanent monitoring regime in place to collect data regularly from distributors on that.

In the last two months, so I think 11th of May, 11th of June, 11th of July, so just over two months it's been in force. It seems to be going okay. We have had inquiries from consumers about whether distributors are correctly applying the rules, and we've talked to two different distributors about how they apply the rules.

So we do think it is going okay and that generally, consumers are getting the 10 kilowatts if they want it, because 10 kilowatts is quite a large installation. So not all consumers can afford or have the roof space for- No... 10 kilowatts, yeah.

There's quite a few that are- That are... outside between 10 and 15, isn't there? Yeah. We've only got time for two more questions. One will be from Joseph Mooney and one will be- Thank you, Madam Chair. I would interestingly, the hedge contracts or the non-discrimination obligations which you've recently brought in, I think 1st of July this year, to try and ensure that, well, particularly for the large generator retailers don't fail their own requirements.

As I understand it, available in four pricing reimbursement contracts. I know you've got the six-month assessment that I think that you put in place to monitor this. I'm just wondering, is this the mechanism that you are intending to use to ensure that these are working, or do you have another process that you intend to use to ensure these NDOs are working as intended?

Can we take that one offline and come back to you on that? I think we probably don't have the detail on that, unless Eric, you have a comment to make on that, I think we'll take it offline and come back to you if there's time. That's fine. That would be great. Just a final question on the part of the complaint which relates to lines companies accessing batteries.

The rules have changed. This is one where there's been a longer runway, so you might be able to provide us with longer insight into whether the core of the policy problem is that some lines companies can use batteries as a tool to build to capacity more efficiently, build to peak more efficiently, but that there might be anti-competitive offshoots of allowing them to do that at scale.

Is that something where the rules have, rule changes, in your view, have led to greater distribution of batteries amongst the lines networks? Thanks, Chair. I can answer that one, too. Okay. There is no restriction or barrier on distributors owning batteries or any of the generation themselves. What there is a threshold- Yeah... above which, which is 50 megawatts, which is actually quite large.

Above that threshold, if they want to do that, then they have to put some protections in place, what we call the arms' length rules, to ensure that any competitor has a reasonable access to be a competitor to their own internal divisions. The rules were under Part 3 of the Electricity Act, and they recently moved into the code. We have the power to grant exemptions, and we had it under the Act, and we still have that power under the code as well.

And we have granted exemptions to two lines companies, distributors- Yeah... to own more than that 50 megawatt threshold without having to put the arms' length rules in place. And the underlying reasons for those, they'll be in our published exemption decisions, but the underlying reasons for those is that the benefit of the arms' length rules was outweighed by the cost.

Yeah. So we granted those exemptions. And those powers work well, and any distributor can apply for an exemption, and they always get assessed on a case by case. There's no precedent effect. Every one's assessed on its merits. And it's a sort of first in, first served as well then because that is precedent setting, so you might have competitors who want to build in Auckland, but they're competing with Line Vector's battery.

Yeah. Any competitor that wants to install in Auckland- Yeah... doesn't have to apply to us. Yeah. Okay? It's only the- They have to get the connection agreement. They have to get the connection agreement. And that is, we've made some pretty big changes to the code, in December last year- Yeah... around those very large connections.

Anything above 300 megawatts, I think. There's some very large changes to make it easier and fairer for those competitors to apply, both more transparency against other competitors as well, so they can all see what's going on, including the distributor's own generation arm if they want to own. And of course, Vector doesn't.

Vector's one of the ones that their generation's well below the threshold. That's great. Yeah. Thank you very much. That's all we have time for. Really have appreciated you coming in. And thank you very much, Eric, and warm wishes to your chair in his new role. Thank you. And pass on the invitation, if you want any further information from the Authority at any time, please reach out.

We're happy to provide that to you and to help you. Thank you. Thank you. Have a great day. Thank you. Thank you. I think that's pretty on time, as far as I can see. We have 15 minutes with you. I'm sure there will be questions. Yeah. But in my experience, the best way that these hearings work is if you spend a little bit of time talking about not only your written complaint, but also why this is motivating- Yeah... for you and what you see as the appropriate remedy.

And then we'll open up for members on both sides to ask you a couple of questions before the end. Okay. All right. I have written something to just keep myself to time. Great. Tena koutou katoa, Madam Chair and members of the committee. Thank you for allowing me to come and speak today. I just want to first acknowledge the clerk's advice that the committee can only consider the secondary legislation that has been made.

So I've narrowed the submission down to just the foundation curriculum policy statements around English and mathematics and statistics under Section 90 of the Education Training Act. So this narrowed submission goes to grounds A and H of the complaint under the standing order. Parliament delegated curriculum-making authority to the minister under Section 90 of the Education and Training Act.

Section 4 of the act states its purposes include establishing and regulating an education system that is high quality, culturally responsive, seamless, and inclusive, and that honors Te Tiriti of Waitangi and supports Māori-Crown relationships. My submission is that a delegated legislative power of this kind is normally expected, I would say, to be exercised in a way that is transparent and traceable through the documentary record so that Parliament and this committee can verify that it's been exercised consistently with that statutory

purpose. The documentary record, which I know I've sent you a bunch of bits of, contains a number of curriculum development documents, design principles, design criteria, consultation records, curriculum development processes, and then the final curriculum statements. The curriculum development record includes different curriculum architectures at different stages. Those include the Understand Know Do, Themes Knowledge Skills, the UKD Progress Outcomes, and then the final Strands Knowledge Practice structure that was used in the final document.

The documentary record also shows different treatments of Te Tiriti of Waitangi by cultural foundations, inclusion and equity across the successive curriculum development document. Development record further shows agreed design principles, criteria, writing groups, quality assurance processes, error review, and other revision process. My submission is that this documentary pathway connecting these elements to the final curriculum statements made under Section 90 is not readily apparent from the record itself.

Mm. The question I guess I'm posing to the committee is whether the documentary record demonstrates that this delegated power has been exercised transparently and in a manner that can be traced through the record. And that's the standard I'm asking the committee to apply under grounds A and H of the complaint. Cool. Okay.

Dr. Jun Nan, do you have a question? I do, but Chair, do you have a question? Yeah, I just- Sure. To start, Dr. Coleman, I wanted to ask you, this is an area that I am an expert in. Yep. And so in the development of the sort of two-phase development where you've got the first being the year zero to six English, the zero to six Te Reo Rangatira, year zero to eight Mathematics and Statistics, and then the second phase- Yeah... which was the public consultation.

Are they both problematic? Is it all problematic, or is the issue that the purpose statement was given a different sort of effect in particularly the language curriculum statements? I'm trying to understand which parts the committee will be best spending its time on understanding, the parts of the complaint that relate to the purpose that was initially made by Parliament.

I think in terms of the... Let's check in terms of which part of it. I would say it's all problematic- Okay... honestly. Yeah. Yeah. I think you would struggle to see how Te Tiriti of Waitangi, for example, has been embedded and is apparent throughout the draft curriculum.

Well, not the draft now, the English curriculum and maths curriculum documents. And that's something that's been commented by other... PBTA and NZED have both lodged submissions around those things. Yeah. Okay. And as we pass through it, comparing this to, say, the last time that curriculum statements would have been made, what's a useful way of comparing Parliament's purpose being given effect in a curriculum statement in the past?

Hmm. I don't know, honestly. I guess the through line that you can see from the purpose of what Parliament exercises into that initial foreword into the curriculum statement- Yeah... I suppose from 2007, and then how that's been carried through the learning areas themselves. Okay. Yeah.

Really helpful. Thank you. Okay. Dr. Jun Nan. Yeah. Thank you, Chair. I guess one of the things, if you're looking at Section 90, which is the empowering position of the curriculum, is that Section 90 is quite broad. It does give ministers a lot of actual genuine powers to kind of do, any ministers, to do all of those things.

But one of the things that whatever happens within the Education Training Act that must be fulfilled is around purpose of the act. Mm-hmm. So we're looking at holding it up to Section 4. As you will know that there are different parts, strands to that purpose. You mentioned in terms of inclusion and Te Tiriti aspect- Mm... which are both the two explicit mentioned aspects of the purpose of the Education and Training Act. Do you find- This is a broader question, but you have more specific questions around the extra supplementary documents that you sent.

Do you find that the way that the framework and the curriculum design has happened actually meets the standard that one would expect of the Ministry of Education, or potentially the government, the Crown, when it comes to the purpose of the Education and Training Act around Te Tiriti inclusion being the first part of my question.

I guess the second part with that, following on from what the chair was asking, is how has previous curriculum designs, if you know, have done things differently to try and meet that standard as expected of the purpose, and that this one, in that sense, doesn't quite meet that standard?

Okay, so I guess the question one is, do I think that it's met the standard of inclusion and equity? And I guess my answer would be no , I don't think it has. And again, that comes down to the lack of visibility of the principles around Te Tiriti o Waitangi throughout the learning area. So not just mentioned in the purpose statement.

I'm talking now about the curriculum document for the learning area of English, for example. But actually how that's carried through into the detail, through the knowledge and practices and all of the different phases of the learning. Similarly, and this is in those documents I submitted around the two clearing design principles, I guess the mention of inclusion and what inclusion meant, going from a recognition of diversity to a more sort of standardized all children encompassing definition.

And just a follow-up question. So in relation to the supplementary document that you've submitted, can I just check? So there are two design principles. Yeah. One on the 19th, I believe. Yeah. And one on the 30th. Which is less than two weeks apart. But the two are quite different.

Yes. This might be quite a simple question. Why are they so different? Okay. So I couldn't answer that question for you. I can tell you how I got these documents, and therefore that might help. These documents are both labeled the 12th of April 2024.

The publicly released version, which is the 19th of April version, I had seen whilst I was working at the Ministry of Education, and that was a document that we were given to say this is the new design principles upon which we will be now developing our work. I was the lead writer for the arts curriculum.

The 30th of April version is also dated the 12th of April. Mm. Is the same number document, but was signed on the 30th of April. It is quite different. The first time I saw that was two weeks ago. It was sent to me as a result of a request for material around the consultation of the current drafts of arts, technology, social sciences, and sciences and learning languages.

I was asking about the consultation process, and I had asked around, what would you be assessing the feedback against? The first response I got mentioned a few things, and it gave me the establishing a knowledge rich curriculum cabinet paper. It did say, "We are also going to hold them against the design criteria." I went back and said, "And what are they?" And they sent me this document.

Oh, okay. I understand. So it doesn't make sense to me in terms of the timeline, but that's how they came to-- Yeah . Okay. I understand. And so then just trying to understand, so that was then public consultation follows, and then later it gets to October '25, which is when the minister's then making a decision about those. So presumably, within that time period, you've gone back and-- Well, the Ministry of Education's been able to go back, consider public feedback, and then there are more changes, and then it comes to the

minister to make that decision, all enabled by Parliament's- Yeah... passing a reading of the- Yeah. So I guess my understanding of that procedure normally-- Well, we did some consultation around the draft work that I was doing in 2023, and that similarly had a process for going. We put some stuff out for consultation, just our initial things with the arts, technology, and science.

NZCER as a research entity, collated that consultation material, wrote a report. The report came to us. Recommendations came to us. We kind of looked at them, didn't negotiate, decided what we were going to respond to, and then responded to that. I don't know what was done with the consultation material from the English.

We probably have time for one or two more questions. I was going to say, I do have follow-up questions. Me too. I just had a single question. Sure. So, I'm just trying to parse out, and from your documents it was really helpful, but just as a global view- Yeah Crown's got to exercise a degree of deference to Te Tiriti o Waitangi- Yeah... as our constitutional document.

At what points were there checks that that was happening? Like the decision-making steps, so they give rise to the judicial review, but we're not really concerned with that. We're concerned with whether Parliament's intent, which should be read alongside Te Tiriti o Waitangi's effect, is part of the purpose.

Is there a built-in part of the process? So I would suggest that, while I was there, in terms of the documents that we were creating during 2023 around curriculum, we had, yes, there was an Oraru Taki group, and there was-... considerable kind of checks with, we had a Māori advisory within the ministry and an inclusion advisory within the ministry that would look at what we were doing and consider it from a disability standpoint, from a languaging standpoint, and then, as I said, there was a specific Māori group that would look at it.

I don't know about this particular piece of work, whether or not that happened. Okay. What I can say is that the version that we saw of the design principles, the 19th version that had a note to Te Tiriti and bicultural foundation is quite typical of something we would have in the Ministry of Education, and a document that didn't have that would've been out of step.

Out of step. Okay, gotcha. Understand. Dr. Junnan. Yeah, I think I'm still stuck on the fact that you got two documents that's dated at the same day, and I'm assuming one of them is the one that's gone to possibly the minister, because I can see the minister has made comments on that particular document. But the other one's the one that stayed with the ministry.

Would that be- Yeah. Is that normal? No. Is that normal that- No. And as I said, I had not seen the document with the minister's handwritten notes on it, I only saw two and a half weeks ago or whenever it was sent to me. And the reason I guess was slightly taken aback is I thought, I've seen this date of this document before, I've seen the title of this document before, I've seen the number of this document before, but it looks very different.

And so no, it was not given to us inside the ministry while I was there. Gotcha. Cool. While you were developing the curriculum? Yes. Okay, cool. Okay. We've run out of time for questions. That's okay. But really, really appreciate you coming in.

Thank you so much for making yourself available. If there's any other things that come to mind, feel free to just give us a short written follow-up. Okay. Awesome. Thank you so much. Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Coleman. Okay.
